summary: A humorous feature on how local musicians blend old and new technology in their work, from retrofitted TVs and body-wired instruments to robot-arm drummers, 3D-printed violins, live-coded DJ sets, virtual concerts and repurposed surveillance gear. It profiles several local artists with dates and mottos in 2023, centered around venues like The Electric Banjo. It concludes that the community is a cocreator of an ever-evolving scene where instruments are limited only by imagination.
one_line: A playful local-arts feature profiling area musicians who build instruments and performances from gadgets, robots, code, virtual venues and surveillance gear.
key_facts: The Electric Banjo is a local pub known for artisanal craft beer and experimental symphonies.
Tim "Twitch" Jackson retrofitted his grandmother's vintage television into a retro-futuristic synthesizer; his creed is "If it beeps, it can bop." The note dates his scene to September 6, 2023.

April Ludgate-Dwyer (no relation to the "Parks and Recreation" character) performed on October 14, 2023 in a leather jacket studded with input and output jacks, wiring herself directly into her instruments.
April Ludgate-Dwyer's latest album is titled "Current Mood: Electric."
Derrick "Digi" O'Sullivan works from a garage at the crossroads of Elm and Main, using salvaged robot arms from the defunct auto industry to drum; his motto is "If it's got a servo, it's got soul!"
Derrick "Digi" O'Sullivan's concert took place on November 3rd.
Melody van Beethoven, a self-described distant relation of the composer, unveiled a 3D-printed violin strung with fiber optic 'strings' on December 18th.
Freddie "Fader" Lee replaced the turntable with a laptop and codes beats live on stage, performing on January 22nd; his maxim is "Why drop the beat when you can compile it?"
Lisa "Laser" Liu and George "Gigabyte" Garrity created a virtual concert series using augmented reality, with avatars and holograms attending, on May 5th.
The anonymous group "The Watchers" repurposes old surveillance equipment as instruments, turning traffic cameras into projectors and tapped phone lines into samples.
On June 9th, it was revealed that The Watchers' old cameras were capturing basslines and hi-hats rather than privacy infringements, leaving the town reeling in rhythm and conspiracy theories.
The article concludes that the community is not just audience but cocreator, and the definition of instruments is only as narrow as our imagination.
